---
title: 'Setting Up Python'
---

Unit 3 uses [Python](https://www.python.org/), in [Jupyter notebooks](https://jupyter.org) (documents that mix code, its output, and explanatory text) [@kluyverJupyterNotebooksPublishing2016]. You write and run code in small cells, one at a time, and see the result immediately below each one, which makes them forgiving for learning: run a cell, see what happens, change it, run it again.

This page covers two things: how much Python you need, and how to get a working setup.

## Required Python Knowledge

You won't write Python from scratch in this unit. You'll read, run, and adapt a notebook that has already been written, and ask an LLM to explain anything that isn't clear ([Coding with LLMs](coding_with_llms.qmd)). But you need to be able to follow what the code is doing. Pick the route that best fits you:

- **You already use Python:** skip ahead to [the setup options](#setup-options).
- **You've used some Python, or another programming language, before:** read the refresher below, and check that each idea in it looks familiar.
- **You've never programmed:** work through the first two units of this [self-paced introduction to Python](https://github.com/gpizzorno/introduction-to-python) before you start the case study. Then read the refresher below, as a check.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## A Quick Python Refresher

Python reads relatively close to plain English. Five ideas are enough to follow the case study:

- **Variables** store a value under a name:

  ```python
  text = 'MY DEAR COLVIN'
  ```

- **Lists** hold a collection of items, in order:

  ```python
  letters = ['wikisource_vol1_ch1_letter1.txt', 'wikisource_vol1_ch1_letter2.txt']
  ```

- **Loops** do something for each item in a list:

  ```python
  for letter in letters:
      print(letter)
  ```

- **Functions** are reusable, named blocks of code. They take inputs and return a result:

  ```python
  def count_words(text):
      return len(text.split())

  count_words(text)  # 3
  ```

- **Libraries** are code that someone else has written, which you import and use. The case study uses `pandas` for tables and `transformers` for the model:

  ```python
  import pandas as pd

  letters = pd.read_csv('../data/letters_metadata.csv')
  ```

Notice the indentation: in Python, the lines that belong to a loop or a function are indented under it. If any of this is unfamiliar, the [self-paced introduction](https://github.com/gpizzorno/introduction-to-python) covers it properly.
:::

## Setup Options

There are three ways to get set up, each in its own tab below. If you're not sure, start with Google Colab.

<div class="table-container table-90">

| Option | Install? | Good for |
|-|-|---|
| Google Colab | No, runs in the browser | Getting started quickly, or a computer where you can't install software |
| Anaconda | Yes, one installer | A permanent local setup, with a graphical launcher |
| Plain Python | Yes, command line | People comfortable with a terminal |
: {.sm}

</div>

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Google Colab

[Google Colab](https://colab.research.google.com) runs notebooks on [Google's computers](https://research.google.com/colaboratory/faq.html), and you see the results in your browser. You only need a Google account.

1. Open the [case study notebook on GitHub](https://github.com/gpizzorno/understanding-ai/blob/main/code/ner_pipeline.ipynb) and click the <span class="command">Open in Colab</span> badge at the top.
2. Run the first cell. It downloads a copy of this repository into your Colab session, so the notebook can find the data.
3. Carry on from there. The libraries the notebook needs are already installed in Colab.

::: {.callout-warning}
## About Colab

Two things to know about Colab:

- **Your session is temporary.** When it ends, the downloaded data and anything you created (such as your annotations) are deleted. Download anything you want to keep (<span class="command">File</span> → <span class="command">Download</span>), or save a copy of the notebook to your Google Drive (<span class="command">File</span> → <span class="command">Save a copy in Drive</span>).
- **Annotations:** to use your own annotations, upload your `my_annotations.csv` file to `understanding-ai/data/annotations/` in Colab's file browser (the folder icon on the left) before running Section 9.
:::

### Anaconda

The [Anaconda distribution](https://www.anaconda.com/download) installs Python, Jupyter, and many common libraries in one go, on Windows, macOS, or Linux.

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## Anaconda Licensing

Anaconda is free for individuals, for teaching, and for organizations with fewer than 200 employees, but [its terms](https://www.anaconda.com/blog/update-on-anacondas-terms-of-service-for-academia-and-research) may require a paid licence for other uses at larger organizations, research included. If that might apply to you, check with your institution, or install [Miniforge](https://conda-forge.org/download/) instead: it's free for everyone, and the steps below are the same, with <span class="command">Miniforge Prompt</span> in place of <span class="command">Anaconda Prompt</span>.
:::

1. Download and run the installer from [anaconda.com/download](https://www.anaconda.com/download). You can install it like any other program (the defaults are fine).
2. Get a copy of this repository: on its GitHub page, click <span class="command">Code</span> → <span class="command">Download ZIP</span> and unzip it (or use `git clone` if you know git).
3. Open <span class="command">Anaconda Prompt</span> (Windows) or <span class="command">Terminal</span> (macOS and Linux), move into the repository folder, and install the libraries the notebooks need (the `.` means *this folder*, the list of libraries is in `pyproject.toml`):

   ```bash
   cd path/to/understanding-ai
   pip install .
   ```

4. Start Jupyter from the same window:

   ```bash
   jupyter notebook
   ```

   Your browser opens with a list of files. Open `code/ner_pipeline.ipynb`.

You can also start Jupyter from the <span class="command">Anaconda Navigator</span> app instead of the command line, but you still need to run step 3 once.

### Plain Python

If you're comfortable with a terminal, you can use a standard Python installation and a *virtual environment* (an isolated set of libraries for this project, so it doesn't interfere with anything else on your computer).

1. Install **Python 3.12** or later.
   - **macOS:** with [Homebrew](https://brew.sh): `brew install python@3.12`, or use the installer from [python.org](https://www.python.org/downloads/).
   - **Windows:** install the Python Install Manager, from [python.org](https://www.python.org/downloads/) or the [Microsoft Store](https://apps.microsoft.com/detail/9NQ7512CXL7T). Then, in Command Prompt, run `py install 3.12`.
   - **Linux:** use your distribution's package manager (for example, `sudo apt install python3 python3-venv`).
2. Get this repository: `git clone https://github.com/gpizzorno/understanding-ai.git`, or download and unzip it from [GitHub](https://github.com/gpizzorno/understanding-ai).
3. Create and activate a virtual environment in the repository folder:

   macOS and Linux:

   ```bash
   cd understanding-ai
   python3 -m venv .venv
   source .venv/bin/activate
   ```

   Windows (Command Prompt):

   ```bat
   cd understanding-ai
   py -m venv .venv
   .venv\Scripts\activate
   ```

4. **Install the libraries** listed in `pyproject.toml`:

   ```bash
   pip install .
   ```

5. **Start Jupyter:**

   ```bash
   jupyter notebook
   ```

Each time you come back, activate the environment again (step 3's last line) before starting Jupyter.
:::

## Checking Your Setup

Whichever option you chose:

1. Open `code/ner_pipeline.ipynb`.
2. Run the first three code cells (the setup cell, the imports, and loading the metadata).
3. If the third cell prints `Total letters in corpus: 462`, you're ready.

**If something goes wrong:**

- **`ModuleNotFoundError`** (for example, `No module named 'transformers'`): a library is missing. Make sure you ran `pip install .` from the repository folder, in the same environment Jupyter is using. In a notebook cell, you can also run `%pip install transformers` (replacing `transformers` with the missing module): [`%pip`](https://ipython.readthedocs.io/en/stable/interactive/magics.html) always installs into the environment the notebook is running in.
- **`FileNotFoundError` for `../data/...`:** the notebook can't find the data. Make sure you opened the notebook from inside the repository's `code/` folder, not a copy saved somewhere else. [Coding with LLMs](coding_with_llms.qmd#from-code-to-result) explains why this matters.
- **Anything else:** copy the full error message into an LLM and ask what it means, as described in [Coding with LLMs](coding_with_llms.qmd).

The first time the notebook loads a model, it downloads a few hundred megabytes, so you'll want to do it from somewhere with a reasonably fast internet connection. Installing the libraries also takes a while, and several gigabytes of disk space.
